rewritten_text:
"And think, ma'am," Oliver said, tears filling his eyes despite his efforts to stop them. "Oh, think how young and good she is, and how much happiness and comfort she brings everyone around her. I'm sure—certain—absolutely certain—that she won't die, for your sake, because you're so good yourself; and for her own sake; and for everyone she makes so happy. Heaven could never let her die so young."

"Hush," Mrs. Maylie said, resting her hand on Oliver's head. "You think like a child, poor boy. Even so, you remind me of my duty. I forgot it for a moment, Oliver, but I hope I may be forgiven. I am old, and I have seen enough illness and death to know the agony of losing those we love. I have seen enough, too, to know that the youngest and best are not always spared to the people who love them. Yet that should comfort us in our grief. Heaven is just, and these things teach us powerfully that there is a brighter world beyond this one, and that we may reach it quickly. God's will be done! I love her, and He knows how deeply!"

Oliver was surprised to see Mrs. Maylie stop her grieving as she spoke, as though by a single effort. She straightened up and grew calm and resolute. He was even more amazed that her strength lasted. Through all the nursing and watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie remained prepared and composed. She steadily carried out every duty that had fallen to her, and even seemed cheerful. But Oliver was young and did not know what strong minds could achieve in difficult times. How could he, when even those who possess such strength so rarely know it themselves?

An anxious night followed. In the morning, Mrs. Maylie's fears proved all too well founded. Rose was developing a high and dangerous fever.

"We must get to work, Oliver, and not surrender to grief that helps no one," Mrs. Maylie said, putting a finger to her lips and looking steadily into his face. "This letter must reach Mr. Losberne as quickly as possible. It must go to the market town, no more than four miles away along the footpath across the field. From there a messenger on horseback must take it directly to Chertsey. The people at the inn will arrange that, and I know I can trust you to make sure it is done."

Oliver could not speak, but his face showed how eager he was to leave at once.

The place seemed to consist of back lanes, ditches, and small gardens, with the air of a rather dull retreat. Wemmick's home was a tiny wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots. Its roof had been cut and painted to resemble a fort mounted with guns.

"All my own work," said Wemmick. "Looks nice, doesn't it?"

I praised it warmly. I think it was the smallest house I had ever seen, with the oddest Gothic windows, most of them false, and a Gothic doorway almost too small to squeeze through.

"That's a proper flagpole, you see," Wemmick said, "and every Sunday I raise a proper flag. Now watch this. After I cross the bridge, I pull it up—like so—and nobody can get across."

The bridge was a plank spanning a ditch about four feet wide and two feet deep. Still, it was lovely to watch him proudly lift it and fasten it in place. His smile showed real pleasure in the task, not merely a habit.

"Every night at nine, Greenwich time," said Wemmick, "the gun goes off. There he is, look! When you hear him fire, I think you'll agree he's a Stinger."

The gun stood in a separate fortress built from latticework. A clever little cover made of waterproof canvas, rather like an umbrella, sheltered it from the weather.

"Then around the back," Wemmick said, "hidden away so it doesn't spoil the military appearance—because I believe that once you've had an idea, you ought to carry it through and maintain it; I don't know whether you agree—"

I told him I certainly did.

"—Around the back I keep a pig, some chickens, and rabbits. I've put together a little growing frame myself, you see, for cucumbers. At supper you can judge the salad I grow. So, sir," Wemmick said, smiling again but also speaking seriously as he shook his head, "if you imagine this little place under siege, we'd last a devil of a long time for food."

He then led me to a garden shelter only about twelve yards away. The path twisted so cleverly that reaching it took quite a while. Our glasses were already set out there. The shelter stood beside an ornamental lake in which our punch was cooling. This round stretch of water had a central island that might have served as our supper salad. Wemmick had installed a fountain in it. Once you started a small mill and removed a cork from a pipe, the fountain spouted with enough force to make the back of your hand quite wet.

He kept pretending Peter had written and told him all those things, but that was a lie. Every last detail came from that young fool we took in the canoe to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane brought out the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud and cried over it. The letter left the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls. It left the tannery, which was doing good business, to Harvey and William, along with other houses and land worth about seven thousand dollars and another three thousand dollars in gold. It also said where the six thousand in cash was hidden in the cellar. The two cheats said they'd fetch it so everything would be honest and open, and told me to bring a candle. We closed the cellar door behind us. When they found the bag, they poured its contents onto the floor, and all those gold coins were a beautiful sight. You should have seen the king's eyes shine! He slapped the duke's shoulder and said:

"Oh, this isn't wonderful or anything! Oh no, certainly not! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, doesn't it?"

The duke agreed. They grabbed at the coins, sifted them through their fingers, and let them fall jingling onto the floor. Then the king said:

"There's no arguing with it: playing brothers to a rich dead man and acting for foreign heirs who've missed out—that's the business for you and me, Bilge. This comes from trusting Providence. In the long run, it's the best approach. I've tried them all, and there's nothing better."

Almost anybody would have been satisfied with that heap and accepted the amount on trust. But no, these two had to count it. They did, and it was four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king said:

"Damn him, what did he do with that four hundred and fifteen dollars?"

They fretted about it for a while and searched everywhere. Then the duke said:

"Well, he was very sick. Probably he made a mistake—that's what I think happened. Best forget about it and say nothing. We can afford to lose it."

"Oh, sure, we can afford it. That's not what bothers me. I'm thinking about the count. We want everything here to look completely honest and open. We want to carry this money upstairs and count it in front of everyone, so nothing looks suspicious. But if the dead man says there's six thousand dollars, you see, we don't want to—"
